lessonTitle: Pick your training route
title: Create your evidence folder
where: Your Windows host · lab notes and browser
action: On the physical host, open File Explorer and create a SONIC-Lab folder with subfolders Installers, Screenshots, Baselines, and Backups. Keep passwords elsewhere.
expected: The four folders exist on storage with sufficient free space.

lessonTitle: Pick your training route
title: Record the version journey
where: Your Windows host · lab notes and browser
action: Create a lab note: VMware Workstation Pro on the host; Windows Server 2019 Desktop Experience on premises; Server 2019 Azure destination; migrate test workload/data; then upgrade that Azure member server to Server 2022.
expected: Your note distinguishes moving an application from moving a whole VM.

lessonTitle: Pick your training route
title: Choose the required route
where: Your Windows host · lab notes and browser
action: Complete the Windows/AD core, SQL core, Azure foundations, and migration core in sidebar order. Leave MECM and high availability extensions until their setup checks pass.
expected: DC01/DC02 and APP01 are prepared before the migration work.

lessonTitle: Understand the map
title: Know what each practice server does
where: Your Windows host · lab notes and browser
action: Open your lab notes on the Windows host. Write DC01 and DC02: manage practice users, sign-in and DNS. Write APP01: hosts the IIS test website and, in the separate help desk class, osTicket. Write SQL01: stores a practice database; it is not a website. Write DEST-DC01: owns the separate migrate.lab.example.test destination domain. Draw each server on VMnet2, then add the matching addresses from the earlier plan. For the DMZ class later, the new private IIS server moves to its own application network and only the gateway sits in the DMZ.
expected: Your notes show each server name, its job, network and address. You can point to the website server without confusing it with a domain controller.

lessonTitle: Prepare your laptop and downloads
title: Confirm Workstation Pro
where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
action: On your physical Windows PC, open VMware Workstation Pro > Help > About. Record the installed version. This course uses Workstation, not vCenter or ESXi.
expected: The product is Workstation Pro and it can create Windows Server 2019 guests.

lessonTitle: Prepare your laptop and downloads
title: Obtain Server 2019 media
where: Your Windows host · web browser for Microsoft Evaluation Center
action: Use the Windows Server 2019 ISO your course or license administrator supplies. For local-only evaluation, open https://www.microsoft.com/evalcenter/evaluate-windows-server-2019 and download the 64-bit ISO. Save it under Installers.
expected: The media is Windows Server 2019, not 2025.

lessonTitle: Prepare your laptop and downloads
title: Choose the media and license path
where: Your Windows host · lab notes and browser
action: Record language, edition, evaluation/licensed status, and whether Desktop Experience is available. The Azure upgrade exercise uses a licensed/pay-as-you-go 2019 Marketplace member VM with a matching 2022 upgrade path.
expected: Your source and destination license choices are written down.

lessonTitle: Prepare your laptop and downloads
title: Check host resources
action: On the host press Ctrl+Shift+Esc > Performance. Record available RAM and disk space. Start a tiny DC at 1 vCPU and 2048 MB RAM; keep a 60 GB growable system disk. A basic IIS test can start at 2 GB RAM; the full help desk uses 4 GB or more. SQL and MECM use their separate requirements. Shut down optional VMs you are not using; leave memory for your Windows host.
expected: The host has enough free resources for the next required pair of VMs.

lessonTitle: Build the isolated VMnet2 network
title: Open Virtual Network Editor
where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
action: On Windows 10 open VMware Workstation Pro. Choose Edit > Virtual Network Editor. Select Change Settings if shown and approve your administrator prompt.
expected: The editor lets you change virtual networks.

lessonTitle: Build the isolated VMnet2 network
title: Create VMnet2 as Host-only
where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
action: Select Add Network, choose VMnet2 and confirm. Select VMnet2 in the list, then select Host-only. Keep Connect a host virtual adapter to this network checked. Do not select NAT or Bridged.
expected: VMnet2 is listed as Host-only. It has no NAT gateway or connection to your physical LAN.

lessonTitle: Build the isolated VMnet2 network
title: Set the private address range
where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
action: With VMnet2 selected, enter Subnet IP 10.50.0.0 and Subnet mask 255.255.255.0. This /24 is the shared address range for DC01 and DC02.
expected: The editor displays 10.50.0.0 and 255.255.255.0 for VMnet2.

lessonTitle: Build the isolated VMnet2 network
title: Turn off VMware DHCP
where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
action: Clear Use local DHCP service to distribute IP addresses to VMs. We will type fixed addresses into the servers ourselves. Select Apply, then OK.
expected: VMnet2 is saved as Host-only with DHCP off. There is no default gateway to record for this isolated network.

lessonTitle: Build the isolated VMnet2 network
title: Write the two-server plan
where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
action: In your notes write DC01 = 10.50.0.10/24 and DC02 = 10.50.0.11/24. Use mask 255.255.255.0 and leave Default gateway blank on both. DC02 will use DC01 at 10.50.0.10 for DNS. Confirm the VMware host adapter does not already use .10 or .11.
expected: Each server has its own address on 10.50.0.0/24. The public internet address is not in either server's adapter settings.

lessonTitle: Build the isolated VMnet2 network
title: Connect the guests to VMnet2
where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
action: When each guest VM exists and is powered off, select it > VM > Settings > Network Adapter. Choose Custom: Specific virtual network > VMnet2 and enable Connect at power on. Keep one network adapter. Return here to check this after any temporary NAT update session.
expected: Both guest adapters use the same VMnet2. After their static-address lessons, their live consoles show DC01 10.50.0.10/24 and DC02 10.50.0.11/24. The DC02 Windows lesson proves replies in both directions before promotion.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Open the new VM wizard
where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
action: On your physical Windows PC, open VMware Workstation Pro. Click File, then New Virtual Machine. Do not do this inside another VM.
expected: The New Virtual Machine Wizard is open.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Choose Typical
where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
action: In New Virtual Machine Wizard, select the radio button Typical (recommended). Click Next >. You should now see Guest Operating System Installation.
expected: The wizard asks how the guest operating system will be installed.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Use manual Windows installation
where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
action: On Guest Operating System Installation, select I will install the operating system later. Click Next >. You should now see Select a Guest Operating System. We attach the ISO later so Easy Install does not choose the Windows edition for you.
expected: The wizard lets you choose a guest OS profile.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Choose the Server 2019 guest profile
where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
action: On Select a Guest Operating System, click Microsoft Windows. Click the Version drop-down arrow. Select Windows Server 2019 from the list. Click Next > to reach Name the Virtual Machine. If that profile is absent, stop and check your Workstation version; do not guess a different OS.
expected: The guest profile says Windows Server 2019.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Name the VM
where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
action: On Name the Virtual Machine, click Virtual machine name, press Ctrl+A, and type DC01. Click Browse beside Location and select your dedicated lab folder on a drive with enough free space. Click OK in the folder chooser. Check the name and location, then click Next >. The next page is Specify Disk Capacity. This name labels the VMware library entry; it does not rename Windows.
expected: The summary uses DC01 and a location you can find again.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Create a new virtual disk
where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
action: On Specify Disk Capacity, click the Maximum disk size (GB) box. Press Ctrl+A and type 60. If Allocate all disk space now is visible, leave its checkbox clear. Select Split virtual disk into multiple files. Click Next >. The Ready to Create Virtual Machine page should now show the planned 60 GB disk; it is created only when you later click Finish. Splitting files controls how the disk is stored; leaving preallocation off lets it grow as data is written.
expected: Ready to Create Virtual Machine shows the planned 60 GB disk. You have not clicked Finish yet.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Set memory and CPU
where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
action: Click Customize Hardware. Select Memory and enter 2048 MB for a tiny practice DC. Select Processors: 1 processor, 1 core. If Windows updates or the desktop are too slow, shut down and raise memory to 4096 MB. These are practice allocations, not production sizing.
expected: The Memory page shows 2048 MB (or your recorded 4096 MB fallback), and Processors shows one total core.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Attach the Server 2019 ISO
where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
action: Select CD/DVD in the hardware list. Choose Use ISO image file, Browse to your Windows Server 2019 ISO, and enable Connect at power on.
expected: The CD/DVD path ends with your Server 2019 ISO filename.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Attach the private VMnet
where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
action: Select Network Adapter. Choose Custom: Specific virtual network and VMnet2 (Host-only) from LAB 03. Enable Connected and Connect at power on.
expected: The VM is attached to the same private lab VMnet as the other lab servers.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Finish and start the VM
where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
action: Click Close, then Finish. Select the new VM in the Workstation library and click Power on this virtual machine. Click inside its console and press a key when the ISO boot prompt appears.
expected: Windows Setup appears inside the VM console.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Start Windows Setup
action: Choose the language you need for the course, time format, and keyboard, then Next and Install now. Use English (United States) media if you will follow the Azure upgrade-media route later.
expected: Setup displays an edition list or asks for a legitimate product key.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Choose Desktop Experience
action: Select Windows Server 2019 Standard (Desktop Experience), or the matching authorized Datacenter (Desktop Experience) edition your course supplies. If using Evaluation for local practice, record that limitation. Click Next and accept the license only if you agree.
expected: The selected line explicitly includes 2019 and Desktop Experience.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Install only on the new blank disk
action: Choose Custom: Install Windows only (advanced). Select the new VM’s blank Drive 0 unallocated space and click Next. This is a clean install in a new VM, not the later Azure in-place upgrade.
expected: Windows copies files, installs, and restarts.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Create the local Administrator password
action: At Customize settings, set and confirm a strong local Administrator password. Save it in your own password manager, then Finish.
expected: The Windows sign-in screen appears.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Sign into the guest
action: Use Workstation VM > Send Ctrl+Alt+Del (or Ctrl+Alt+Insert), then sign in as the guest’s local Administrator.
expected: You see a Windows desktop and Server Manager.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Install VMware Tools
where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro; then the named Windows guest
action: In Workstation select VM > Install VMware Tools. In the guest open File Explorer > This PC, open the VMware Tools CD, and run setup64.exe if offered. Choose the normal setup and restart when asked.
expected: After restart, the guest is usable with the expected mouse/display integration.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Patch the new Server 2019 guest
where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro; then the named Windows guest
action: This new guest is not domain-joined yet. Shut it down. In VMware choose VM > Settings > Network Adapter > NAT, keeping one adapter. Start Windows and set Ethernet IPv4 and DNS to Obtain automatically for this temporary update session. Open Start > Settings > Update & Security > Windows Update, check for updates and restart as required. Activate the evaluation while internet access is available. Shut down again, change the same adapter to Custom > VMnet2, and start the guest. The next network steps restore its planned static address and blank gateway before any domain work.
expected: Windows has completed its pending restarts.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Rename Windows
action: Inside the guest press Win+R, enter sysdm.cpl, and press Enter. On Computer Name choose Change. Enter DC01, confirm OK, and restart when prompted.
expected: After signing in again, hostname returns DC01.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Open the guest IPv4 settings
action: Inside the guest press Win+R, type ncpa.cpl, and press Enter. Right-click the connected Ethernet adapter > Properties. Select Internet Protocol Version 4 (TCP/IPv4), then Properties.
expected: The IPv4 address and DNS fields are visible.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Enter the lab address
action: For the example LAB 03 network only, choose Use the following IP address: 10.50.0.10; subnet mask 255.255.255.0; leave Default gateway blank (VMnet2 is host-only). Set preferred DNS to 10.50.0.10. Click OK and Close. If you changed the subnet in LAB 03, use your matching address plan instead.
expected: ipconfig /all shows the planned 10.50.0.x address, blank default gateway, and the lab DNS address on VMnet2.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Confirm this is Server 2019
action: Open Start, search Windows PowerShell, right-click it > Run as administrator. Run the read-only inventory below in this VM.
command:
hostname
Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object WindowsProductName, WindowsVersion, OsBuildNumber
DISM /online /Get-CurrentEdition
expected: WindowsProductName identifies Windows Server 2019; hostname identifies DC01.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Open Add Roles and Features
action: Inside the named server open Server Manager. Choose Manage > Add Roles and Features. Click Next on Before you begin.
expected: The Select installation type page is shown.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Select the local destination server
action: Choose Role-based or feature-based installation > Next. Select a server from the server pool and select this VM’s computer name > Next.
expected: The Server Roles page targets the correct computer.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Select AD DS and its tools
action: Check Active Directory Domain Services. In the pop-up click Add Features, then Next.
expected: AD DS is selected and its required management tools are included.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Install the role
action: Keep the required Features selected. Click Next through the AD DS information page, review the selected target, then click Install.
expected: Installation succeeds and offers Promote this server to a domain controller.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Choose the correct promotion operation
action: Click Promote this server to a domain controller. Choose Add a new forest. Enter lab.example.test as Root domain name. Click Next.
expected: The wizard shows a NEW forest named lab.example.test.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Set controller options and DSRM
action: For Server 2019 in this lab, use Windows Server 2016 for both forest and domain functional levels. Keep DNS server and Global Catalog selected. Set and confirm a unique DSRM recovery password, store it securely, then Next.
expected: Required options are selected and the password boxes have no validation error.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Review DNS and additional options
action: Continue past the isolated-root DNS-delegation warning only if it is the expected warning for this private lab. Confirm the LAB NetBIOS name on Additional Options.
expected: The wizard advances without a blocking validation error.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Keep the default AD paths
action: On Paths keep the default NTDS database/log and SYSVOL locations for this small lab, then Next.
expected: The wizard shows Review Options.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Check prerequisites before promotion
action: On Review Options confirm lab.example.test, the correct computer, and DNS. Click Next, then wait for Prerequisites Check.
expected: The prerequisite check succeeds; only understood lab warnings remain.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Promote and wait for restart
action: Click Install only after the prerequisite check passes. Wait for the VM to restart; do not power it off to shorten the wait.
expected: The guest restarts and offers a domain sign-in.

lessonTitle: Make DC01: the agency begins
title: Verify the directory
action: Sign in with your authorized lab.example.test administrator account. Open Windows PowerShell as administrator in this VM and run the checks.
command:
hostname
Get-ADDomain | Select-Object DNSRoot, NetBIOSName
Resolve-DnsName -Type SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.lab.example.test
expected: The DNSRoot is lab.example.test and domain-controller records resolve to the lab’s private IPs.

lessonTitle: Create test users, OUs, and a GPO
title: Open Active Directory Users and Computers
action: Inside DC01 open Server Manager > Tools > Active Directory Users and Computers. Expand lab.example.test in the left pane.
expected: You are managing the lab.example.test directory on DC01.

lessonTitle: Create test users, OUs, and a GPO
title: Create the Operations OU
action: Right-click lab.example.test > New > Organizational Unit. Enter Operations. Leave protection from accidental deletion enabled, then OK. Repeat to create Security.
expected: Both OUs appear under lab.example.test.

lessonTitle: Create test users, OUs, and a GPO
title: Create the test user
action: Right-click Operations > New > User. Enter a fictional name and user logon name test.analyst. Click Next, set a private temporary password, choose your lab password-change requirement, Next, then Finish.
expected: test.analyst appears in Operations.

lessonTitle: Create test users, OUs, and a GPO
title: Create and populate the group
action: Right-click Operations > New > Group. Name it GG-Operations, select Global and Security, then OK. Open the group > Members > Add; enter test.analyst > Check Names > OK.
expected: Members lists the new test user.

lessonTitle: Create test users, OUs, and a GPO
title: Open Group Policy Management
action: In Server Manager choose Tools > Group Policy Management. Expand Forest: lab.example.test > Domains > lab.example.test.
expected: The Operations OU appears in the policy tree.

lessonTitle: Create test users, OUs, and a GPO
title: Create and link the GPO
action: Right-click Operations > Create a GPO in this domain, and Link it here. Name it LAB-Operations-Banner and click OK.
expected: The named GPO is linked under Operations.

lessonTitle: Create test users, OUs, and a GPO
title: Edit the logon banner
action: Right-click the linked GPO > Edit. Expand Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options. Set the interactive logon message title to LAB LAB and message text to This is a practice environment.
expected: The two banner settings show your lab text.

lessonTitle: Create test users, OUs, and a GPO
title: Verify the objects
action: On DC01 run these read-only checks and capture ADUC plus the GPO link.
expected: The user, group membership, and GPO are returned.

title: Start on your own Windows computer
where: Your Windows computer at home · web browser
action:
Use the Windows computer you will use to connect to the lab. Open your browser and go to https://portal.azure.com. Sign in with the Azure account used in the earlier lessons.

An NSG, short for Network Security Group, is a list of network traffic rules. Inbound means coming into the Azure VM. Outbound means leaving it. Your connection leaves your Windows computer and arrives at the VM, so the VM needs an INBOUND rule.

where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
action:

whoami
$env:COMPUTERNAME

$SonicUserSid

title: Inspect the owner and who can read the key
where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
action:
icacls lists the file’s permission entries. R means read, W means write, M means modify, F means full control, and I means inherited from the parent folder. Inheritance means a file receives permissions from its folder.
Get-Acl shows the owner and a table of entries. Allow gives access; Deny blocks access. Check the file itself and its parent folder. Removing inheritance does not remove permissions that were added directly to the file.
For your personal client key, use your own account as owner and restrict access to that account under workplace policy. Reading is enough for SSH to use it. Other ordinary users or shared groups should not read it. Do not copy Windows SSH server authorized_keys permission recipes onto this personal private key.
If the owner is another account, the file is centrally managed, or access is denied, stop and ask the Windows administrator to repair this exact file. Do not take ownership of a folder tree. If elevation is required, reopen PowerShell with Run as administrator under the intended identity and recheck whoami first.
Keep keys under %USERPROFILE%\.ssh, outside OneDrive and the repository. If this key is in a synced/shared folder, arrange a move to that local folder while preserving working access. After moving it, repeat the path-selection and inspection cards with its new path before continuing. Moving it does not erase older shared or cloud copies; replace an exposed key through your normal key-rotation process.
command:
icacls "$SonicKey"
$SonicKeyFolder = [System.IO.Path]::GetDirectoryName($SonicKey)
icacls "$SonicKeyFolder"
(Get-Acl -LiteralPath $SonicKey).Owner
(Get-Acl -LiteralPath $SonicKey).Access | Select-Object IdentityReference, FileSystemRights, AccessControlType, IsInherited
expected: You know the owner, your account SID and the exact unwanted entries before changing anything.

title: Save the current permissions before editing
where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
action:

Push-Location temporarily opens the key’s parent folder so the saved filename can be restored to the same folder later. Pop-Location returns to your previous folder.
If saving fails, stop. Do not continue with an unknown recovery path.

$SonicAclFolder = Join-Path $env:LOCALAPPDATA "SONIC"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $SonicAclFolder -Force | Out-Null
$SonicAclBackup = Join-Path $SonicAclFolder ("key-acl-" + [guid]::NewGuid().ToString() + ".txt")
$SonicKeyName = [System.IO.Path]::GetFileName($SonicKey)
Push-Location -LiteralPath $SonicKeyFolder
icacls "$SonicKeyName" /save "$SonicAclBackup"
$SonicAclSaved = $LASTEXITCODE
Pop-Location
if ($SonicAclSaved -ne 0) { throw "ACL backup failed: stop" }
$SonicAclBackup
expected: The permission backup was saved successfully and its path is recorded.

where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user

title: Inspect the owner and who can read the key
where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
action:

Other ordinary users or shared groups should not read it. Do not copy Windows SSH server authorized_keys permission recipes onto this personal private key.
If the owner is another account, the file is centrally managed, or access is denied, stop and ask the Windows administrator to repair this exact file. Do not take ownership of a folder tree. icacls "$SonicKey"
$SonicKeyFolder = [System.IO.Path]::GetDirectoryName($SonicKey)

(Get-Acl -LiteralPath $SonicKey).Owner
(Get-Acl -LiteralPath $SonicKey).Access | Select-Object IdentityReference, FileSystemRights, AccessControlType, IsInherited

title: Save the current permissions before editing
where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
action:

$SonicAclFolder = Join-Path $env:LOCALAPPDATA "SONIC"

where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
action:

expected: Your explicit read entry exists. Review any remaining explicit entries in the next step.

lessonTitle: Make the first SSH connection as rexuser
title: Remove only a confirmed unwanted explicit entry
where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
action:

lessonTitle: Match the installation method to the artifact
title: Command 1: read, type, then check
where: Reference examples · commented, do not execute
action:
# makes each example a shell comment. These placeholders demonstrate methods; they are not a request to install anything now.
chmod changes permission bits. u+x adds execute permission for the owner only. ./script.sh uses ./ to mean a file in the current directory, not one found through PATH. Review contents, source, integrity, and required interpreter before execution.
bash ./script.sh is an alternative that asks Bash to read the script; it normally needs read permission rather than an execute bit. It does not make a malicious script safe, and not every .sh file is meant for Bash.
sudo requests privileged execution. dnf install ./package.rpm installs a local RPM and resolves dependencies through configured repositories; ./ distinguishes the local file from a repository package name. Review package signature/source and the transaction before confirming.
tar handles archives. -t lists members, -x extracts, -z processes gzip compression, and -f says the next argument is the archive filename. Use listing before extraction and an empty staging directory; untrusted paths, links, or overwrite targets need review. Extraction alone does not install software.
Repository-based dnf install package-name selects a named package from enabled repositories. Trust the repository and package signatures, inspect the proposed transaction, and record the exact installed version.
command:
# Reviewed shell script, two alternative invocation methods:
# chmod u+x ./script.sh
# ./script.sh
# OR: bash ./script.sh
# Reviewed local RPM:
# sudo dnf install ./package.rpm
# Inspect archive before extraction:
# tar -tzf archive.tar.gz
# tar -xzf archive.tar.gz
# Approved repository package:
# sudo dnf install package-name
expected: You can explain the correct method and inspection requirements for each artifact type without changing system state.

lessonTitle: Checkpoint: what is your rollback plan?
title: Before anything changes: decide exactly what to back up
where: Work administration workstation · change record and Veeam console (12 or 13)
action:
Start with the VM you will change: select its whole-VM backup, including the OS disk and every data disk used by the application. For a new RHEL installation, back up the clean, working VM before installing Wazuh. After successful installation and verification, create a new accepted baseline; retain the pre-change recovery point according to policy.
If the change affects AD, DNS, domain membership or Group Policy, verify a recent application-aware backup of the domain controller first, including the volumes containing AD DS, SYSVOL and DNS-related state. Record domain-recovery access and the approved AD recovery procedure. A DNS export or GPO export alone cannot recover a domain controller. Do not casually revert a production domain controller snapshot.
For the Wazuh central host, include its OS, configuration, certificates, enrollment material and all disks containing indexer/event data. If manager, indexer and dashboard are separate VMs, identify all of them. A live disk copy is not automatically a consistent Wazuh/indexer backup: use the application recovery procedure or a coordinated clean shutdown in an approved outage. Do not independently restore mismatched cluster members.
For the RHEL endpoint or Windows client, include the OS, application data and agent configuration before agent installation, realm changes or hardening. Record its current manager association so recovery does not leave duplicate or stale enrollment. Back up only the affected systems and dependencies; an endpoint-only change does not require backing up every enterprise VM.
Save a protected change record outside the changed VM: hostnames, IP/DNS settings, disk inventory, package/kernel versions, service status, relevant configuration and rollback triggers. Keep credentials, private keys and recovery passwords in approved secret storage, never in the course GitHub repository. File hashes and screenshots are evidence, not backups.
expected: A named list of affected VMs, all required disks, dependencies and application-consistency requirements exists before a backup job is selected.

lessonTitle: Checkpoint: what is your rollback plan?
title: Verify the backup scope and recovery access before taking a snapshot
action:
Open Home → Jobs → Backup. Select the existing job → Edit. On Virtual Machines, confirm the exact VM is included; inspect exclusions and disk selection so required data disks are not omitted. Inspect Storage for the intended repository and retention. Use Cancel after read-only inspection; have the backup owner apply any required job changes.
For a Windows domain controller, inspect Guest Processing → application-aware processing and the per-VM application settings. Confirm guest credentials and processing success in the completed session, rather than merely seeing a checked option. Windows AD processing does not make an arbitrary Linux application consistent.
Check that the backup repository is outside the VM being changed, has capacity and remains reachable during recovery. Confirm the restore operator can access the backup and its encryption password independently of the affected machine/domain. Follow the workplace policy for an independent protected or immutable copy.
Ask the backup owner to verify the Veeam server configuration backup too. In the main menu select Configuration Backup and inspect its latest success, repository and encryption setting. This protects backup configuration; it does not replace VM backups. Store its encryption password separately in approved storage. Do not change enterprise backup settings as part of an endpoint lesson.
Run the approved VM backup using the later cards, verify the new per-VM restore point, and record a tested restore route. Only then take a short-lived vSphere snapshot immediately before the change if required. Backup first, temporary snapshot second, change third. This is a pre-change protection order, not a universal disaster-recovery restore order.
expected: The current restore point covers the intended data, recovery access works, and application-specific restore limitations are recorded. Unknown coverage is a no-go.

lessonTitle: Checkpoint: what is your rollback plan?
title: At work: select the exact vSphere VM and recovery scope
action:
Sign in to the approved vCenter URL. Open Menu → VMs and Templates. Select the intended RHEL VM and compare its name, folder, host and disks with the change record. Do not act on a similarly named production VM.
Open Snapshots → Manage Snapshots and inspect existing checkpoints. Check datastore free space and whether a backup job is running. Coordinate the maintenance window with the backup owner; do not take or remove a checkpoint during an active backup.
Record change scope, rollback trigger, maximum diagnosis time, snapshot expiry, backup restore point and validation steps. This RHEL procedure is not a domain-controller recovery procedure: AD needs application-aware/system-state recovery planning and identity consistency.
expected: The change targets one identified RHEL VM and has an independent backup/recovery plan.

lessonTitle: Checkpoint: what is your rollback plan?
title: At work: create a short-lived vSphere snapshot
action:
Right-click the selected VM → Snapshots → Take Snapshot. Enter a unique name containing the change ID and time, and a description of the pre-change state.
For a planned cold checkpoint, shut down the guest cleanly first and confirm Powered off. Memory capture does not apply while powered off. For an approved powered-on checkpoint, decide whether memory capture is needed; it increases size/time. Filesystem quiescing requires working VMware Tools and is not automatically application-consistent backup.
Select Create/OK. Watch Recent Tasks until the snapshot task succeeds, then reopen Manage Snapshots to confirm its name/time. Record the evidence before starting the change.
Keep snapshots brief and remove them after validation and approval. Broadcom advises not retaining a single snapshot beyond 72 hours; workplace policy can require a shorter period. Snapshot deltas depend on base disks, so they are not standalone backups.
expected: The intended checkpoint exists and its owner, expiry and consistency limitations are recorded.

lessonTitle: Checkpoint: what is your rollback plan?
title: At work: choose fix, revert or restore from backup
where: Work administration workstation · change record and vSphere Client
action:
If the change works, validate the application and document the result. If it fails, preserve logs and make one evidence-based correction within the agreed time. If risk grows or the time expires, stop and execute the recorded recovery branch.
For an approved snapshot revert: right-click the exact VM → Snapshots → Manage Snapshots. Select the recorded pre-change checkpoint → Revert. Read the warning about losing later changes and confirm only within the approved outage/data-loss scope. Verify power state, guest access, storage and application behavior afterward.
For cleanup after a successful change: select the checkpoint → Delete. Deleting merges snapshot changes; it does not restore the earlier state. Monitor the task and datastore capacity. Do not select Delete All merely to remove one checkpoint.
If snapshots cannot meet the recovery requirement, use the enterprise backup restore plan. Test a recovery to an isolated destination when possible; never connect a duplicate restored identity to production by accident.
expected: Recovery is judged by validated guest/application state, not just a completed hypervisor task.

lessonTitle: Checkpoint: what is your rollback plan?

where: Approved Veeam administration machine · Veeam PowerShell session
action:
Open the Veeam console → Help → About and record the product, version and build. These command names refer to Veeam Backup & Replication VMware VM jobs; Veeam Agent jobs and other Veeam products use different cmdlets.
Open the PowerShell session supplied with the installed Veeam console. Run Get-Command to discover what is available, then Get-Help for the local syntax. Do not run these in the RHEL terminal or assume ordinary Windows PowerShell already has the Veeam module.
Get-VBRJob inspects VM jobs; Get-VBRBackupSession inspects execution history; Get-VBRRestorePoint inspects recovery points. Starting a job is a separate authorized operation, not proof of recovery. The exact start/restore walkthrough must match your workplace version and job type.
command:
Get-Command Get-VBRJob, Get-VBRBackupSession, Get-VBRRestorePoint, Start-VBRJob
Get-Help Get-VBRJob -Full
Get-Help Start-VBRJob -Full
expected: The product/build and supported local command syntax are identified before any backup job is changed or started.

lessonTitle: Checkpoint: what is your rollback plan?
title: At work: inspect one existing VMware backup job
where: Veeam Backup & Replication · Veeam PowerShell session
action:
This example targets an existing VMware VM backup job, not a Veeam Agent policy. Verify these cmdlets in your installed version first. In the console select Home → Jobs → Backup and copy the exact approved job name.
Enter that name at the prompt. Get-VBRJob retrieves jobs; Where-Object keeps only an exact name match. The count check stops an ambiguous selection. Review the returned job in the console and confirm it includes the intended VM, the correct repository, retention and application-processing settings.
Get-VBRBackupSession lists history. It does not create a backup. Inspect the job session and per-VM task results in History; an old successful run is not proof of a current restore point.
command:
$SonicJobName = Read-Host "Exact approved VMware backup job name"
$SonicJobs = @(Get-VBRJob | Where-Object { $_.Name -eq $SonicJobName })
if ($SonicJobs.Count -ne 1) { throw "Expected exactly one job: stop" }
$SonicJob = $SonicJobs[0]
$SonicJob | Format-List Name, JobType
Get-VBRBackupSession | Sort-Object CreationTime -Descending | Select-Object -First 10 JobName, CreationTime, EndTime, State, Result
expected: One reviewed job is selected and its VM membership and recent task results are understood.

lessonTitle: Verify the endpoint RPM before installation
title: Download and validate on Windows before transfer
action:
Open Windows Terminal → PowerShell. Create a staging folder under your local profile. Paste the exact official RPM URL and the separate vendor SHA-512 value at the prompts. The digest must contain 128 hexadecimal characters; paste only the digest, not the filename.
Invoke-WebRequest downloads without executing the RPM. Get-FileHash calculates SHA-512 over the downloaded bytes. The comparison ignores hexadecimal letter case. Stop on an exception: check filename, release, architecture and algorithm, then download again from the official source. Never change the expected digest to make a failed check pass.
A vendor checksum checks against published bytes; it does not replace the signing-key and RPM signature checks below. Keep the digest in your change record.
command:
$SonicStage = Join-Path $env:USERPROFILE "sonic-artifacts"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $SonicStage | Out-Null
$SonicRpm = Join-Path $SonicStage "wazuh-agent.rpm"
$SonicUrl = Read-Host "Exact official HTTPS RPM URL"
$SonicExpected = (Read-Host "Vendor SHA-512 digest only").Trim()
if ($SonicUrl -notmatch "^https://packages\.wazuh\.com/") { throw "Use the official package URL" }
if ($SonicExpected -notmatch "^[0-9a-fA-F]{128}$") { throw "Invalid SHA-512 value" }
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri $SonicUrl -OutFile $SonicRpm
$SonicActual = (Get-FileHash -LiteralPath $SonicRpm -Algorithm SHA512).Hash
if ($SonicActual -ine $SonicExpected) { throw "CHECKSUM MISMATCH: do not transfer or install" }
Write-Output "VENDOR SHA-512 MATCH"
$SonicActual
expected: VENDOR SHA-512 MATCH appears before you transfer anything.

where: Your Windows host · lab notes and browser
action: Back up important files to a separate device or service and restore one sample. Save recovery keys for existing encrypted disks privately. Start with a new VM; do not repartition your Windows system.
expected: The restored sample opens and the existing OS remains untouched.

lessonTitle: Plan Your Everyday Linux Desktop
title: Size the practice VM
where: Your Windows host · lab notes and browser
action: Plan 2 virtual CPU cores, 4 GB RAM minimum for this exercise (8 GB if your host can spare it), a new 50 GB virtual disk, and NAT networking. Leave resources for Windows.
expected: The host can run one GNOME VM without exhausting RAM or storage.

lessonTitle: Plan Your Everyday Linux Desktop
title: Plan a later physical installation
where: Your Windows host · lab notes and browser
action: Only after validating the VM, test a live environment if available and consult the current installation guide for Wi-Fi, audio, GPU, printers, encryption and disk layout. Keep backups and Windows recovery media.
expected: You have a hardware test list and a recovery route.

lessonTitle: Install AlmaLinux with GNOME
title: Verify the downloaded ISO
action: Download the DVD ISO and CHECKSUM from almalinux.org using official mirror links. In Windows PowerShell compute its SHA-256 and compare with the exact filename in CHECKSUM; check official signature guidance when available. Replace the example ISO path in the command with the exact file you downloaded.
expected: The complete SHA-256 matches the official checksum for your downloaded ISO.

lessonTitle: Install AlmaLinux with GNOME
title: Create a fresh VM
where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
action: In VMware Workstation Pro choose File → New Virtual Machine → Typical → I will install the operating system later. Choose a compatible RHEL 9 64-bit guest profile (or AlmaLinux 9 if offered), name ALMA-DESKTOP, and create a NEW 50 GB virtual disk.
expected: A new VM appears in the library with a blank disk.

lessonTitle: Install AlmaLinux with GNOME
title: Attach media and networking
where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
action: Before power-on open VM Settings. Set 2 cores and your planned RAM. On CD/DVD attach the verified AlmaLinux 9 DVD ISO and enable Connect at power on. On Network Adapter select NAT.
expected: The VM summary shows the correct ISO, memory, and NAT.

lessonTitle: Install AlmaLinux with GNOME
title: Start the installer
action: Power on and select Test this media & install AlmaLinux 9 if available. Choose your language, keyboard and time zone on Installation Summary.
expected: You reach the installer summary without a media-check error.

lessonTitle: Install AlmaLinux with GNOME
title: Select GNOME and the correct disk
action: Open Software Selection and choose Server with GUI. Open Installation Destination, select ONLY the new 50 GB virtual disk, and use automatic partitioning for this practice VM. Review any pending deletion list before accepting.
expected: Only the new VM disk is selected and Server with GUI is the software profile.

lessonTitle: Install AlmaLinux with GNOME
title: Create your daily user
action: Open User Creation, choose your own username and strong password, and enable Make this user administrator (wheel privileges). Keep root credentials private if you set them. Enable the NAT interface in Network & Host Name, then begin installation.
expected: The installer accepts a normal administrative user and completes.

lessonTitle: Install AlmaLinux with GNOME
title: Boot the installed system
action: Reboot when prompted, detach the ISO if it starts setup again, and sign in to GNOME as your normal user. Open Activities, search Terminal, and check the release.
expected: The guest reports AlmaLinux 9 and opens a GNOME desktop.

lessonTitle: Configure Your Desktop
title: Set the basics
action: Open Settings from the system menu. In Displays choose a readable resolution; in Keyboard/Region & Language verify layout; in Sound select output and test it. In Power choose sensible screen blanking.
expected: Typing, display scaling and sound suit your setup.

lessonTitle: Configure Your Desktop
title: Confirm networking
action: In Settings → Network check the wired connection. NAT normally supplies DHCP and DNS. Check addresses and routes without changing them.
command:
ip -br address
ip route
nmcli device status
expected: You have an address and default route for the VM NAT connection.

lessonTitle: Configure Your Desktop
title: Update the guest
action: In Terminal refresh package metadata and review the proposed update transaction before accepting. Save work, then reboot when the update finishes.
expected: The transaction completes without unresolved errors and GNOME returns after reboot.

lessonTitle: Configure Your Desktop
title: Install VMware desktop integration
action: Inspect/install the distribution guest tools. Review the transaction, then log out and back in or reboot. Keep shared folders and host clipboard sharing off unless you intentionally need them.
expected: GNOME can resize appropriately when supported by your Workstation settings.

lessonTitle: Configure Your Desktop
title: Set lock and privacy
action: In Settings → Privacy configure Screen Lock. Review Location and file-history options. Press Super+L and confirm the lock screen, then unlock with your own password.
expected: The desktop locks and unlocks as expected.

lessonTitle: Configure Your Desktop
title: Record a clean baseline
where: AlmaLinux VM · GNOME Settings; then VMware Workstation Pro on your host
action: Open About and note release, memory and disk. Shut down the VM, then take a named Workstation snapshot if your edition supports it; separately keep backups of important files.
expected: You have a starting point note and a VM recovery checkpoint.

lessonTitle: Learn the Commands You Use Every Day
title: Know where you are
action: Open Terminal and check your identity and location. Read each command and output before moving on. ~ means your home directory, not the whole filesystem.
expected: You recognize your own username, host and home path.

lessonTitle: Learn the Commands You Use Every Day
title: Make a practice folder
action: Create a practice folder under your home and move into it. mkdir -p creates missing parent directories. Use Tab to complete names and the Up arrow to recall a command.
expected: pwd ends with DesktopPractice and the folder is inside your home.

lessonTitle: Learn the Commands You Use Every Day
title: Create, copy and rename
action: Write two lines to a practice text file. > replaces that named file; do not aim it at valuable files. Copy first, then rename the copy.
command:
cd ~/DesktopPractice
printf "first line\nsecond line\n" > notes.txt
cp -i notes.txt copy.txt
mv -i copy.txt renamed.txt
cat renamed.txt
expected: You have notes.txt and renamed.txt with the same two lines.

lessonTitle: Learn the Commands You Use Every Day
title: Search and inspect
action: Find files and filter text. A pipe sends one command’s output into the next. Use less to page through longer output and press q to leave.
command:
cd ~/DesktopPractice
grep -n "second" notes.txt
wc -l notes.txt
find . -maxdepth 1 -type f
ls -lah | less
expected: grep returns the matching line and wc counts two lines.

lessonTitle: Learn the Commands You Use Every Day
title: Learn help and interruption
action: Use --help or man for syntax; q exits man. Ctrl+C interrupts a foreground task; Ctrl+Shift+C copies selected text in GNOME Terminal. Never paste a command you cannot explain.
expected: You can find an option’s meaning and exit a pager.

lessonTitle: Learn the Commands You Use Every Day
title: Clean only your practice copy
action: Use interactive removal for the renamed practice copy. Confirm only after checking its full path, then verify the original remains. Avoid rm -rf as a routine cleanup habit.
expected: notes.txt remains and the chosen practice copy is gone.

lessonTitle: Manage Files and Permissions
title: Navigate with Files
action: Open Files from Activities. Open Home, Documents and Downloads. Ctrl+L enters a path; type ~/DesktopPractice and Enter. Ctrl+H toggles hidden files.
expected: You can locate the same practice file from GUI and Terminal.

lessonTitle: Manage Files and Permissions
title: Create and organize
action: In Files create an Everyday folder in Documents. Copy notes.txt into it, rename the copy, and open it with the text editor. Use Trash for unwanted practice copies.
expected: Your copied document opens and the original is still present.

lessonTitle: Manage Files and Permissions
title: Understand permissions
action: Check a file you own. Apply mode 600 to the practice notes only: owner read/write, no access for group/others. This is not full-disk encryption.
expected: ls shows owner-only read/write on that practice file.

lessonTitle: Manage Files and Permissions
title: Create an archive
action: Use Files → right-click the Everyday folder → Compress (menu labels can vary). Choose a ZIP filename. Extract it into a temporary folder and open the copied note.
expected: The extracted note matches your original.

lessonTitle: Manage Files and Permissions
title: Use removable storage
action: Connect a USB data drive and open its entry in Files. Copy a harmless sample, wait for transfer completion, then use Eject/Unmount before disconnecting.
expected: The sample reopens and the drive disconnects without a busy warning.

lessonTitle: Install and Maintain Everyday Apps
title: Inspect your existing software sources
action: DNF manages system RPMs and dependencies. GNOME Software may show RPM and Flatpak sources. List enabled DNF repositories and check package details before installing.
command:
dnf repolist
dnf info firefox
dnf search libreoffice
expected: You know which repositories are currently enabled.

lessonTitle: Install and Maintain Everyday Apps
title: Install a native everyday app
action: For an office suite use the AlmaLinux repository package libreoffice if available. Read the package source, extra packages the app needs and download size, then approve the install. Start it from Activities.
expected: A document opens in the installed app.

lessonTitle: Install and Maintain Everyday Apps
title: Install Flatpak support
action: Install the Flatpak client from your configured AlmaLinux repositories. Then check existing user remotes. System and user remotes are different scopes.
command:
sudo dnf install flatpak
flatpak --version
flatpak remotes --user
expected: flatpak is available and your user remote list is visible.

lessonTitle: Install and Maintain Everyday Apps
title: Add Flathub only after reviewing the source
where: AlmaLinux VM · web browser for Flathub; then GNOME Terminal
action: Open the official Flathub AlmaLinux setup page linked below. If you accept this third-party source, add it to your user only. Check its URL afterward.
expected: The user-scoped flathub remote points to the official source.

lessonTitle: Install and Maintain Everyday Apps
title: Install an app and review permissions
action: Search for VLC, check the exact Flathub app ID and source, then install the user-scoped example only if you accept its publisher and permissions. Launch from Activities or Terminal.
command:
flatpak search VLC
flatpak remote-info --user flathub org.videolan.VLC
flatpak install --user flathub org.videolan.VLC
flatpak info --user --show-permissions org.videolan.VLC
flatpak run org.videolan.VLC
expected: VLC starts and opens a non-sensitive local media sample.

lessonTitle: Install and Maintain Everyday Apps
title: Update and remove deliberately
action: Update RPMs with DNF and user Flatpaks separately. Before removing an app, review extra packages the app needs and preserve needed data. Flatpak uninstall without --delete-data normally leaves user app data.
command:
sudo dnf upgrade --refresh
flatpak update --user
flatpak list --user --app
expected: You can explain the two update paths and identify an app’s source.

lessonTitle: Install Steam and Understand Proton
title: Check hardware and game support first
where: Your Windows host · lab notes and browser
action: Read the game’s official Linux/Steam requirements. Check GPU support and the current Steam/Proton information. Anti-cheat, DRM and Windows-only launchers may prevent play; some games require Windows.
expected: You selected one compatible test title and recorded the hardware expectation.

lessonTitle: Install Steam and Understand Proton
title: Inspect and install Steam from Flathub
action: Check the exact Steam application ID on Flathub and its permissions. The Flatpak wrapper is community maintained. Review requirements and accept the install only if it fits your system.
command:
flatpak remote-info --user flathub com.valvesoftware.Steam
flatpak install --user flathub com.valvesoftware.Steam
flatpak info --user --show-permissions com.valvesoftware.Steam
expected: Steam is installed in your user Flatpak scope.

lessonTitle: Install Steam and Understand Proton
title: Start and sign in
action: Launch Steam from Activities or Terminal and let its client updates finish. Sign in privately; never capture the password, QR code or Steam Guard code for evidence.
expected: You reach your own Steam Library.

lessonTitle: Install Steam and Understand Proton
title: Try a native title first
action: Choose a small Linux-native title that meets the VM or physical machine’s graphics capability. Pick the default library location, check required space, and download it. Launch and record the actual result.
expected: The supported test game launches, or you record the specific compatibility failure.

lessonTitle: Install Steam and Understand Proton
title: Test Proton separately
action: In Steam → Settings → Compatibility check Steam Play/Proton options. For a compatible Windows title, use its Properties → Compatibility to choose an offered supported Proton version when needed. Test one title at a time.
expected: You can distinguish native Linux execution from a Windows game using Proton.

lessonTitle: Install Steam and Understand Proton
title: Keep libraries and runtimes healthy
action: Update user Flatpaks and Steam. Use Steam Settings → Storage to view library usage. For an external library first complete the WD storage class and grant only that path to the Steam sandbox.
expected: You know where the game is stored and how much free space remains.

lessonTitle: Configure Network, Printing and Sharing
title: Inspect network before changing it
action: Use Settings → Network or Wi-Fi for your connection. A VMware VM usually sees virtual Ethernet even when Windows uses Wi-Fi. Check active connections and addresses.
command:
nmcli connection show --active
ip -br address
ip route
expected: You identify the right adapter and active connection.

lessonTitle: Configure Network, Printing and Sharing
title: Separate DNS from connectivity
action: Resolve a known official site, then test HTTPS. If name lookup fails but your network route exists, check the connection’s DNS details before changing anything.
command:
getent hosts almalinux.org
curl -I https://almalinux.org
nmcli device show
expected: You can tell a name-resolution error from an HTTPS or connection error.

lessonTitle: Configure Network, Printing and Sharing
title: Add a printer
action: Open Settings → Printers, unlock if requested, choose Add, and select an allowed detected printer or its confirmed IPP address. Print a single test page.
expected: The queue exists and the actual test page prints.

lessonTitle: Configure Network, Printing and Sharing
title: Configure peripherals
action: In Settings → Bluetooth pair one device if supported. Test input/output under Sound. In a VM pass through a specific USB device only when needed, then disconnect it when finished.
expected: The chosen device works, or its unsupported state is documented.

lessonTitle: Configure Network, Printing and Sharing
title: Access a known file share
action: In Files → Other Locations enter the approved smb://server/share address. Use an account authorized for that share and test with a harmless file. Disconnect afterward.
expected: The authorized share opens without changing server permissions.

lessonTitle: Add Storage from a Western Digital Drive
title: Identify how the drive reaches AlmaLinux
where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
action: On a physical AlmaLinux PC connect the intended USB drive, or power off and follow the PC manual for an internal SATA installation. In VMware, USB passthrough can attach an external disk exclusively to the guest. For learning, prefer adding a separate NEW virtual disk while powered off. Never use raw access to your Windows system disk.
expected: The drive appears in AlmaLinux without formatting or partition changes.

lessonTitle: Add Storage from a Western Digital Drive
title: Match model, serial and capacity
action: Open Activities → Disks. Select the candidate drive and record its model, serial, size and partitions. Compare with the physical device label. Check terminal output too; do not assume /dev/sdb is always the WD drive.
expected: You positively distinguish the data drive from the system disk mounted at /.

lessonTitle: Add Storage from a Western Digital Drive
title: Use an existing data volume without erasing it
action: If it contains files, select its existing partition in Disks and use Mount (play button), or open it from Files. Do NOT choose Format Disk, Format Partition or Delete. Record the actual mount path from Disks and check your own files.
expected: Existing files are visible and unchanged.

lessonTitle: Add Storage from a Western Digital Drive
title: Prove copy access and available space
action: For a writable mounted volume copy only your harmless notes.txt using Files, reopen it, and compare its SHA-256 with the source. In Terminal quote the ACTUAL mounted path when using df -h or findmnt -T. Do not run a placeholder as a path.
expected: The sample file matches and free space is shown for that mounted filesystem.

lessonTitle: Add Storage from a Western Digital Drive
title: Optional: prepare a NEW empty practice disk
action: Skip this step for any drive containing data. On a separate practice blank virtual disk, reconfirm identity in Disks, use its menu → Format Disk → GPT if a partition table is needed, then the + button → Create Partition → choose ext4 for Linux-only practice and a label such as PracticeData. Formatting ERASES selected content; review the device and deletion prompts before confirming.
expected: Only the explicitly empty practice disk has the new Linux filesystem.

lessonTitle: Add Storage from a Western Digital Drive
title: Choose persistent mounting only if needed
action: Existing removable drives can simply mount from Files when plugged in. For a dedicated Linux data disk, in Disks select the partition → gear → Edit Mount Options; record the existing options, use stable UUID identification, a deliberate path such as /mnt/WDData, and nofail for an optional disk. Test while attached before a reboot. Do not edit the root mount.
expected: The chosen data volume mounts at its intended path and the machine still boots.

lessonTitle: Add Storage from a Western Digital Drive
title: Understand what space you added
action: A disk mounted at /mnt/WDData increases storage available at that path; it does not enlarge /. Keep files there intentionally. On a new empty ext4 practice mount only, use Files as an administrator or a reviewed one-directory ownership change for your user; never recursively chown an existing data tree.
expected: You can explain which filesystem gains files and which remains unchanged.

lessonTitle: Add Storage from a Western Digital Drive
title: Use it for games or disconnect it safely
action: For Steam use a Linux-native dedicated library folder on this mounted drive. Grant only that ACTUAL folder to the user Steam Flatpak (via a permissions manager or reviewed flatpak override --user --filesystem=EXACT_PATH com.valvesoftware.Steam), then add the library in Steam Settings → Storage. When done close apps and unmount/eject before unplugging.
expected: The correct library path is visible, or the data volume ejects cleanly.

lessonTitle: Back Up Your Desktop and Restore a File
title: Choose what matters
where: Your Windows host · lab notes and browser
action: List Documents, Pictures, project files, browser exports and game saves you need. Include needed hidden app data deliberately. Do not assume an installed app is the same as its documents.
expected: You have a short backup scope and destination.

lessonTitle: Back Up Your Desktop and Restore a File
title: Make a dated sample backup
action: In Files create a dated backup folder on your verified external destination. Copy the Everyday folder and practice notes. Wait for completion, then safely unmount the destination.
expected: The copied files exist on a different device.

lessonTitle: Back Up Your Desktop and Restore a File
title: Prove restore without overwriting
action: Reconnect the destination and copy the sample into ~/RestoreTest using Files. Open it and compare hashes for the original and restored file.
command:
sha256sum ~/DesktopPractice/notes.txt
# Also hash your actual restored file path; compare the full values.
expected: Restored content matches and opens.

lessonTitle: Back Up Your Desktop and Restore a File
title: Schedule a repeatable habit
where: AlmaLinux VM · backup notes and calendar
action: For this first class, use the manual Files backup you just tested. Set a weekly reminder in your calendar to copy the chosen folders into a new dated folder on your backup drive. Keep earlier copies until you check the new one. Write down when you last restored a sample, where the backup lives and who can unlock any encryption. You can choose an automated backup tool later; do not call a scheduled copy a tested backup until you have restored from it.
expected: Your plan says when to back up and how to recover.

lessonTitle: Back Up Your Desktop and Restore a File
title: Keep VM snapshots separate
where: Your Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
action: Use powered-off VM snapshots for short experiment rollback, and separate backups for valuable data. Review snapshot growth and remove obsolete snapshots using Workstation’s supported manager.
expected: You can explain rollback versus independent file recovery.

lessonTitle: Troubleshoot Everyday Linux Problems
title: State the problem precisely
action: Record what failed, when, the app, the last change, and whether it happens to all users or one. Reproduce using a harmless action and capture the exact error.
expected: You have one testable problem statement.

lessonTitle: Troubleshoot Everyday Linux Problems
title: Check resources
action: Check space, memory and running processes. In top press q to exit. A full filesystem can break updates and app state.
expected: You can identify the filesystem or process actually consuming resources.

lessonTitle: Troubleshoot Everyday Linux Problems
title: Inspect services and recent errors
action: Read failed units and the current boot’s warning/error journal. Journal access can require authorized sudo; check before changing a service.
expected: You can relate an error timestamp and service to the symptom.

lessonTitle: Troubleshoot Everyday Linux Problems
title: Inspect one service deliberately
action: For an actual named failed service, use systemctl status SERVICE and journalctl -u SERVICE -b. Replace SERVICE with the real unit from your previous check. Research the specific error before a restart.
expected: You know the failing dependency/configuration or what saved result is missing.

lessonTitle: Troubleshoot Everyday Linux Problems
title: Respect SELinux and firewall boundaries
action: Check SELinux state and active firewall policy. If an app is denied, check its logs and the official supported labeling/port guidance. Do not disable SELinux or firewalld as the default workaround.
expected: You recorded current protection state without weakening it.

lessonTitle: Troubleshoot Everyday Linux Problems
title: Recover and prove the fix
action: Reverse only the identified change, restore an app config backup, or use the VM recovery checkpoint if necessary. Repeat the original test and save before/after evidence.
expected: The original problem is resolved or narrowed with clear next evidence.

lessonTitle: Connect to Real AlmaLinux Terminal Output
title: Understand where commands execute
where: Your Windows host · lab notes and browser
action: The hosted website is copy/help mode. GNOME Terminal runs Bash inside your AlmaLinux VM. The local SONIC companion starts PowerShell on Windows; its WSL tab is a separately installed WSL distro, NOT your VMware VM.
expected: You can name the machine each shell controls.

lessonTitle: Connect to Real AlmaLinux Terminal Output
title: Install Node.js and Git, then start the local app
action: On your Windows host, open Start, type Windows PowerShell and open it. Follow the linked terminal setup guide to install Node.js LTS (which includes npm) and Git with its PowerShell commands. Close and reopen PowerShell or use the guide’s PATH refresh command. Run node --version, npm.cmd --version and git --version before continuing. In File Explorer, open the downloaded academy project folder, click its address bar, type powershell and press Enter: that opens PowerShell in the correct project folder. Run the block below there; npm.cmd avoids a blocked npm.ps1 script without weakening your execution policy.
command:
Set-Location $env:USERPROFILE
git clone --branch main https://github.com/CloudSeamTech/SONIC-Academy.git
Set-Location .\SONIC-Academy
npm.cmd ci
npm.cmd run dev
expected: SONIC opens on localhost, normally port 3000.

lessonTitle: Connect to Real AlmaLinux Terminal Output
title: Start the companion in a second Windows window
action: From the same repository root in a second PowerShell window install the packages the companion needs and start it. Keep this process open. The random pairing token is private and stays on your computer.
command:
npm.cmd run companion:install
npm.cmd run companion:start
expected: The companion prints a loopback address and pairing token.

lessonTitle: Connect to Real AlmaLinux Terminal Output
title: Connect and prove a real Windows result
where: Your Windows host · web browser at http://localhost:3000/migration#view=terminal
action: At http://localhost:3000/migration#view=terminal select Windows PowerShell. Paste the token into the local-only field and Connect locally. Run Get-Date twice. Compare with your own Windows clock.
expected: Live date/time output appears from your current Windows account.

lessonTitle: Connect to Real AlmaLinux Terminal Output
title: Optionally enable SSH inside the AlmaLinux guest
action: For VMware access use GNOME Terminal to install/start the SSH server and check its address and firewall. If SSH is not already allowed, add the ssh service only to the active connection’s firewall zone after checking it. This opens private-network SSH access; NAT needs no public port-forward. In firewall-config select the active zone and check the ssh service only for that private connection, then make the reviewed change permanent if needed. Alternatively use firewall-cmd --zone=<your-active-zone> --add-service=ssh, replacing the placeholder; repeat with --permanent only after testing.
command:
sudo dnf install openssh-server
sudo systemctl enable --now sshd
ip -br address
sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all
expected: sshd is active and you know the guest’s actual NAT address.

lessonTitle: Connect to Real AlmaLinux Terminal Output
title: Verify host identity and connect from Windows
where: AlmaLinux VM · Terminal; then Windows host · PowerShell
action: In the guest check the ED25519 host-key fingerprint. In Windows PowerShell use ssh your-user@the-actual-guest-IP and compare the offered fingerprint before accepting. The text user/IP are placeholders; substitute your own. Use native PowerShell for a full interactive SSH session; the SONIC panel can relay basic prompts but is not a full-screen terminal emulator.
command:
sudo ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub
# Above: AlmaLinux guest only. Then run ssh with your actual user/IP in Windows.
# After SSH connects: whoami; hostname; cat /etc/os-release
expected: You reach the intended AlmaLinux host and can verify its release and username.

lessonTitle: Connect to Real AlmaLinux Terminal Output
title: Use the right terminal and shut down cleanly
where: AlmaLinux VM · GNOME Terminal; then local academy browser on your Windows host
action: Run AlmaLinux desktop commands in GNOME Terminal or your verified SSH session. Use exit to leave SSH. In SONIC choose Disconnect and stop the companion process with Ctrl+C when finished. Stop the local dev server separately.
expected: Remote/local prompts are distinguishable and the companion is no longer listening when stopped.
